A model explaining how distance from a market shapes what crops/land uses surround it.
Farming done mainly to feed the farmer's own household, not for sale.
Mid-20th-century spread of high-yield seeds, fertilizer, and irrigation to developing regions.
Growing a single crop over a large area of land.
A location where goods transfer between transport modes, often spurring city growth (e.g., a port).
Burgess's model describing a city growing outward in rings from a central business district.
An influx of wealthier residents into a lower-income neighborhood, often displacing existing residents.
A country's largest city, disproportionately larger than all its other cities.
A composite measure combining life expectancy, education, and income to rank development.
A model describing a linear sequence of stages countries pass through while industrializing.
Shifting production to another country, typically to reduce labor costs.
The decline of manufacturing in a formerly industrial region.
Absolute: exact coordinates (latitude/longitude). Relative: position compared with other places.
The environment sets limits, but people choose how to respond to it.
Shrinking of distance's effect as transport and communication speed up.
Crude birth rate minus crude death rate (excludes migration).
Doubling time ≈ 70 ÷ annual growth rate (%).
Shift in leading causes of death from infectious to chronic diseases as societies develop.
Refugees flee across a border; internally displaced persons stay inside their own country.
Rapid person-to-person spread through a population (viral video, disease).
The idea spreads but the trait changes to fit the new culture (McAloo Tikki).
A shared language used between speakers of different languages.
Adapting a global product or idea to local culture.
Unitary: power concentrated nationally. Federal: power shared with regional governments.
A border drawn before an area was heavily settled.
A state's claim to territory where its ethnic group lives in another state.
States giving up some sovereignty to a larger body, like the EU.
Mechanization and better techniques that coincided with the Industrial Revolution.
Slash-and-burn farming in tropical areas; plots are abandoned as soil declines.
Integration of farming with corporate processing, distribution and marketing.
An area with poor access to affordable, nutritious food.
Site: physical characteristics of a place. Situation: its location relative to other places.
Hoyt: wedge-shaped zones extending outward along transport routes.
Harris & Ullman: a city grows around several separate centers.
Denying loans or insurance in certain neighborhoods, often by race.
Primary: extraction. Secondary: manufacturing. Tertiary: services. Quaternary: knowledge/information.
Industry locates to minimize transport, labor and agglomeration costs.
Area with tax breaks and relaxed rules to attract foreign investment.
Meeting present needs without compromising future generations.
The study of where things are on Earth and why, for both people and the physical environment.
Visual tools for spatial information: maps, graphs, charts, diagrams, photos.
A system for classifying things into groups, such as types of regions or diffusion.
The physical world not made by people: climate, landforms, soil, water, vegetation.
The natural environment as modified by people: farms, roads, buildings (cultural landscape).
Shared beliefs, values, language, customs, and material traits of a group.
Adopting some traits of another culture while keeping much of your own.
Geography's whole-picture approach combining physical and human factors and many disciplines.
Discredited idea that the physical environment controls human behavior and development.
A flat representation of part or all of Earth's surface; always simplified and distorted.
The science and art of mapmaking / the person who makes maps.
General maps showing locations of places and features (political, physical, topographic).
Reference map showing boundaries, capitals, and cities.
Reference map showing natural features such as mountains, rivers, and elevation.
Reference map showing elevation with contour lines.
Maps showing the spatial pattern of one topic or variable.
Lines connect points of equal value (temperature, pressure, elevation).
Areas shaded by a data value; works best with rates.
Areas resized in proportion to a statistic such as population.
Ratio of map distance to real distance; large scale = small area, more detail.
Keeps shape and direction (navigation) but exaggerates area near the poles.
Parallels measuring distance north or south of the equator, 0°–90°.
Meridians measuring distance east or west of the Prime Meridian, 0°–180°.
About 180° longitude; crossing westward adds a day, eastward subtracts one.
0° longitude, through Greenwich, England.
0° latitude, dividing the Northern and Southern Hemispheres.
Time at the Prime Meridian; the reference for world time zones (now UTC).
24 zones about 15° of longitude wide, because Earth turns 15° per hour.
Projection that keeps relative area accurate but distorts shape.
Equal-area projection showing true continent sizes with stretched shapes.
The physical characteristics of a place itself (harbor, hill, water supply).
A place's location relative to other places (trade routes, access).
Increasing interconnection of economies, cultures, and people worldwide.
A region defined by people's perceptions, with fuzzy borders ('the South').
The spread of a trait or idea from one place to others over time.
Spread through people moving and carrying the trait with them.
Spread outward from the hearth while staying strong there (contagious, hierarchical, stimulus).
How a phenomenon is arranged across space: density, concentration, pattern.
How often something occurs per unit of area.
Total population ÷ total land area.
Farmers ÷ arable land; high = little mechanization.
How spread out a feature is: clustered = close together; dispersed = far apart.
The geometric arrangement of objects: linear, grid, random.
Land suitable for growing crops (about 10% of Earth's land).
An official population count; the U.S. holds one every 10 years.
Computer system that layers and analyzes geographic data.
Compares amounts across categories; read the axis units and bar heights.
Shows change over time; describe direction and rate.
Each dot is one place with two values; shows correlation, not cause.
Temperature line plus monthly precipitation bars describe a climate.
Arrow width is proportional to the volume of movement.
Interaction between places falls as the distance between them grows.

PART_A.q: A map that shows a small area in great detail (e.g., a single neighborhood) is best described as which kind of scale?
o: Small scale
Large scale
Absolute scale
Formal scale
PART_A.e: Large-scale maps show a small area in more detail; small-scale maps show a large area with less detail.

PART_A.q: Which statement best describes a functional region?
o: An area unified by an official, measurable trait like national borders
An area organized around a central node or focal point, like the coverage area of a radio station
An area defined only by people's shared perceptions and feelings
An area with no internal variation whatsoever
PART_A.e: A functional region is organized around a node/focal point (e.g., the delivery zone of a newspaper).

PART_A.q: The concept that interaction between two places decreases as the distance between them increases is called:
o: Space-time compression
Distance decay
Distribution
Site
PART_A.e: Distance decay describes declining interaction/influence as distance grows.

o: A style of hand-drawn cartography
Software that layers multiple spatial data sets for analysis
A single satellite used for remote sensing
A type of population pyramid
PART_A.e: GIS (Geographic Information Systems) layers and analyzes spatial data sets.

PART_A.q: A region defined by shared feelings and cultural identity rather than official data, such as 'the South,' is a:
o: Formal region
Functional region
Perceptual region
Political region
PART_A.e: A perceptual (vernacular) region is based on people's mental image/shared perception of an area.

PART_A.q: Which measure of population density divides total population by only the farmable land in a country?
o: Arithmetic density
Physiological density
Agricultural density
Areal density
PART_A.e: Physiological density divides population by arable land, better reflecting pressure on farmland.

PART_A.q: A country with a wide, triangular-shaped population pyramid is most likely in which stage of the demographic transition?
o: Stage 1
Stage 2
Stage 4
Stage 5
PART_A.e: A wide-based, triangular pyramid reflects high birth rates and rapid growth, characteristic of Stage 2.

PART_A.q: In Stage 2 of the demographic transition model, population grows rapidly mainly because:
o: Birth rates rise sharply
Death rates fall while birth rates remain high
Both birth and death rates fall together
Migration into the country surges
PART_A.e: Stage 2 growth is driven by falling death rates (sanitation/medicine) while birth rates stay high.

PART_A.q: Conditions that attract migrants to a destination, such as job availability, are known as:
o: Push factors
Pull factors
Intervening obstacles
Distance decay
PART_A.e: Pull factors draw migrants toward a destination.

PART_A.q: A Total Fertility Rate of approximately 2.1 is generally considered:
o: Far below replacement level
Replacement level
Evidence of a primate city
A sign of rapid urbanization
PART_A.e: A TFR near 2.1 is considered 'replacement level' — enough to keep population roughly stable, absent migration.

PART_B1.q: The spread of a cultural trait through direct, physical movement of people who carry it is:
o: Contagious diffusion
Hierarchical diffusion
Relocation diffusion
Stimulus diffusion
PART_B1.e: Relocation diffusion occurs when people physically move and bring a trait with them.

PART_B1.q: A new fashion trend that starts in a major global city and spreads down through smaller cities is an example of:
o: Stimulus diffusion
Hierarchical diffusion
Relocation diffusion
Contagious diffusion
PART_B1.e: Hierarchical diffusion spreads from places/people of power or influence downward to others.

PART_B1.q: A religion that actively seeks converts everywhere and appeals to all people, regardless of location, is classified as:
o: An ethnic religion
A universalizing religion
A folk religion
A hearth religion
PART_B1.e: Universalizing religions (e.g., Christianity, Islam, Buddhism) seek converts across all populations.

PART_B1.q: The point of origin of a cultural trait or innovation is called its:
o: Hearth
Isogloss
Toponym
Node
PART_B1.e: A hearth is the place where a cultural trait or innovation originates.

PART_B1.q: Judging another culture by the standards and values of one's own culture is:
o: Cultural relativism
Syncretism
Ethnocentrism
Acculturation
PART_B1.e: Ethnocentrism is evaluating another culture through the lens of one's own cultural standards.

PART_B1.q: A boundary that was forcibly drawn over an existing cultural landscape, often ignoring it, is called:
o: An antecedent boundary
A subsequent boundary
A superimposed boundary
A relic boundary
PART_B1.e: Superimposed boundaries are drawn (often by an outside colonial power) without regard to existing cultural patterns.

o: A state gaining new territory through conquest
A central government granting more autonomy to regions within the state
Two states merging into one
A state losing all sovereignty to a supranational body
PART_B2.e: Devolution is the transfer of increased autonomy from a central government to regional governments.

PART_B2.q: Which of these is an example of a centripetal force within a state?
o: A widely shared national language
A strong separatist movement
Uneven regional economic development
Ethnic conflict between regions
PART_B2.e: A shared national language unifies a state and strengthens cohesion — a centripetal force.

PART_B2.q: The practice of drawing electoral districts to concentrate opposition voters into as few districts as possible is called:
o: Cracking
Packing
Devolution
Superimposition
PART_B2.e: 'Packing' concentrates opposition voters into few districts, reducing their overall influence.

PART_B2.q: A state whose population shares a single, unifying cultural identity that matches its political borders is best described as a:
o: Multinational state
Nation-state
Stateless nation
Supranational organization
PART_B2.e: A nation-state is a state whose borders closely align with a single nation's cultural identity.

PART_C.q: Written response: choose TWO concepts from different units and construct an argument connecting them. Cite specific evidence from each.
o: Names both concepts precisely, gives concrete evidence for each, and explains the causal/logical bridge
Lists the two topics without connecting them
Describes only one concept in detail
Gives a personal opinion with no course evidence
PART_C.e: Strong responses anchor every claim in specific unit content and explain how the two concepts connect.

workedExamples.title: Natural increase rate
workedExamples.prompt: A country has a crude birth rate of 24 and a crude death rate of 8 (per 1,000 people). Find the natural increase rate and doubling time.
steps: NIR = (CBR − CDR)/10, as a percent = (24 − 8)/10 = 1.6%
Doubling time ≈ 70 / 1.6 ≈ 44 years

workedExamples.title: Population density
workedExamples.prompt: A region has 3,000,000 people on 1,500 km², of which 300 km² is farmland. Find the arithmetic and physiological densities.
steps: Arithmetic density = people / total land = 3,000,000 / 1,500
Physiological density = people / arable land = 3,000,000 / 300

workedExamples.title: Dependency ratio
workedExamples.prompt: A country has 25% of people under 15, 65% ages 15–64, and 10% over 64. Find the dependency ratio.
steps: Dependents = under 15 + over 64 = 25 + 10 = 35
Ratio = dependents / working-age × 100 = 35/65 × 100

workedExamples.title: Identifying scale
workedExamples.prompt: A study of voting patterns in one county is at what scale?
steps: Scale of analysis is the area a study covers: global, regional, national, state or local
Voting patterns within one county cover a small, bounded area
So the scale of analysis is local, even though results may be compared to national patterns

workedExamples.title: Explaining cultural diffusion
workedExamples.prompt: How did hip-hop spread around the world?
steps: It began in the Bronx in the 1970s.
Media and the internet spread it, an example of hierarchical and contagious diffusion.
Local artists adapted it with their own languages and styles.
workedExamples.answer: Hip-hop diffused through media and was reshaped locally.

workedExamples.title: Using the concentric zone model
workedExamples.prompt: Describe Burgess's concentric zone model of a city.
steps: The central business district is at the core.
Surrounding it are rings: transition, working-class housing, middle-class homes and commuters.
The city grows outward from the center.
workedExamples.answer: The city is organized in rings around a central business district.

workedExamples.title: Applying Weber's least-cost theory
workedExamples.prompt: Why do steel mills tend to locate near coal and iron ore?
steps: Raw materials such as iron ore lose weight when processed.
Moving heavy raw materials is expensive.
Locating near them minimizes transportation costs.
workedExamples.answer: Locating near raw materials reduces the cost of transport.

workedExamples.title: Centripetal and centrifugal forces
workedExamples.prompt: Identify one centripetal and one centrifugal force in Belgium.
steps: Centripetal forces unify a state, such as shared national institutions and the capital Brussels.
Centrifugal forces divide a state, such as the language divide between Flemish and French speakers.
Federalism is one way Belgium manages these tensions.
workedExamples.answer: Brussels and federalism unify, while language differences divide.

workedExamples.title: Using Von Thunen's model
workedExamples.prompt: Where would dairy farming be located relative to a city?
steps: Milk is perishable and costly to transport.
Von Thunen predicts intensive, perishable products close to the market.
Land near the city is expensive, so only high-value uses locate there.

workedExamples.title: Calculating Three Kinds of Density
workedExamples.prompt: A country has 60 million people, 300,000 km² of land, 20,000 km² of arable land, and 3 million farmers. Find the arithmetic, physiological and agricultural densities.
steps: Arithmetic density = people ÷ total land = 60,000,000 ÷ 300,000 = 200 people/km²
Physiological density = people ÷ arable land = 60,000,000 ÷ 20,000 = 3,000 people/km² of arable land
Agricultural density = farmers ÷ arable land = 3,000,000 ÷ 20,000 = 150 farmers/km² of arable land
Compare: a physiological density much higher than the arithmetic density means little of the land is arable

workedExamples.title: Time Zone Calculation
workedExamples.prompt: It is 9:00 am Monday at the Prime Meridian. What is the time and day at 120°E, and at 90°W?
steps: Each 15° of longitude is one hour
120°E: 120 ÷ 15 = 8 hours EAST (ahead): 9:00 am + 8 h = 5:00 pm Monday
90°W: 90 ÷ 15 = 6 hours WEST (behind): 9:00 am − 6 h = 3:00 am Monday
Crossing the International Date Line (180°) would change the date

workedExamples.title: Using a Map Scale
workedExamples.prompt: A map has a scale of 1:100,000. Two towns are 7.5 cm apart on the map. How far apart are they in real life?
steps: Convert to meters: 750,000 cm ÷ 100 = 7,500 m
Convert to kilometers: 7,500 m ÷ 1,000 = 7.5 km

hardQuiz.q: A map shades each U.S. county in a darker color where population per square mile is higher. Which type of thematic map is this?
o: Dot map, which uses one symbol to represent a set number of people
Isoline map, which connects points of equal value using continuous lines
Choropleth map, which shades defined areas according to a data value
Topographic map, which shows landforms with contour lines
hardQuiz.e: A choropleth shades predefined areas such as counties by data classes. An isoline map is tempting because it also shows a continuous variable, but it uses lines through points of equal value, not shaded areas.

hardQuiz.q: A surveyor records a courthouse at 32.78 degrees N, 79.93 degrees W. Which type of location is this, and why?
o: Absolute location, because it uses a fixed global coordinate grid
Relative location, because it describes position by distance to other places
Site, because it describes the physical characteristics of the place itself
Situation, because it describes the place's connections to surrounding areas
hardQuiz.e: Latitude and longitude give an exact, unchanging absolute location. Relative location is tempting but depends on describing the place in relation to other places, which coordinates do not do.

hardQuiz.q: Since 2015, millions of people have left Venezuela. Which pair of conditions is an example of push factors behind this emigration?
o: Job openings and higher wages in neighboring Colombia
Hyperinflation and shortages of food and medicine
Relatives who are already settled in Chile or Spain
A promise of political freedom and safety abroad
hardQuiz.e: Push factors are negative conditions in the origin that drive people away, such as hyperinflation and shortages. Job openings abroad are tempting but are pull factors that attract migrants to a destination.

hardQuiz.q: Which example illustrates hierarchical diffusion?
o: Measles spreading from child to child through a school over the course of several weeks
Korean immigrants bringing food traditions with them to Los Angeles
A new mobile phone plan spreading house by house through a single suburb
A style endorsed by famous influencers spreading to the wider public through followers
hardQuiz.e: Hierarchical diffusion passes from people or places of influence to others. Measles spreading child to child is tempting but is contagious diffusion, which depends on proximity and not on rank or authority.

hardQuiz.q: According to von Thunen's model, why are dairy and vegetable farms located closest to a city?
o: Soil quality is highest near cities, so higher yields offset the transport costs there
High land rent near the market favors perishable, intensively produced goods
Low land rent near the market allows large areas to be used for grazing
Transport costs matter little, so farmers choose products by climate alone
hardQuiz.e: Competition for land near the market raises rent, so farmers use it intensively for perishable, costly-to-transport goods. The low-rent answer is tempting but reverses the model, in which rent falls with distance from the market.

hardQuiz.q: A model describes a city with a zone in transition of factories and low-income housing around the CBD, and incomes rising in rings farther outward. Which model is this?
o: Concentric zone model (Burgess)
Sector model (Hoyt), with wedges of land use along transport routes
Multiple nuclei model (Harris and Ullman), with several separate centers
Galactic city model, with edge cities around a beltway
hardQuiz.e: Burgess described rings of land use outward from the CBD, with a transition zone and rising income farther out. The sector model is tempting but arranges land uses in wedges along routes, not in rings.

hardQuiz.q: A firm makes steel from iron ore and coal, both of which lose much of their weight during processing. According to Weber's least-cost theory, where will it most likely locate?
o: Near the market, because the finished steel weighs more than the inputs
Near its rivals, to gain agglomeration benefits at the expense of lower transport costs
Near the raw materials, to minimize the cost of moving weight-losing inputs
Near the largest labor pool, whatever the weight of the inputs involved
hardQuiz.e: Weber's theory minimizes transportation, labor, and agglomeration costs, and weight-losing inputs favor a site near the materials. Locating near the market is tempting but applies to products that gain weight, not to steel here.

hardQuiz.q: A country earns most of its export revenue from copper and imports manufactured goods from wealthy countries. In core-periphery models, what is a likely result for this country?
o: It sets global copper prices through large banks in its capital city
Export earnings swing with core demand, limiting its bargaining power
It gains most of the value added by processing copper into finished goods
It relies on its domestic market and avoids dependence on foreign investment
hardQuiz.e: Peripheral economies that export raw materials depend on demand and prices set in the core, which limits their bargaining power. The value-added answer is tempting but reverses the pattern, since the core captures profits from manufacturing.

hardQuiz.q: A government expels a foreign military from its territory and sets its own immigration laws. Which concept does this best illustrate?
o: Self-determination, the right of a nation to govern itself without outside interference
Irredentism, a claim to territory held by a neighboring state
Devolution, the transfer of power to regional governments
State sovereignty, the exercise of supreme authority within recognized borders
hardQuiz.e: Sovereignty means a state controls what happens within its recognized territory. Self-determination is tempting but concerns the right of a nation to form its own state, not a state's authority over its existing territory.

hardQuiz.q: When Greece adopted the euro, it could no longer set its own monetary policy. What does this show about membership in a supranational organization like the European Union?
o: Members cede some decision-making authority to a body above the state level
Members merge their governments into one state with a single capital and one leader
Members must adopt a shared national language and culture
Members must end trade with countries outside the organization
hardQuiz.e: Supranational organizations ask states to give up some authority in specific areas while remaining separate states. Merging into a single state is tempting but the EU's members keep their own governments and sovereignty in most areas.

hardQuiz.q: According to the graph, which country’s farmland is under the greatest pressure?
o: Country X
Country Z
Country Y
They are equal, since all three have similar arithmetic densities
hardQuiz.e: Physiological density (people per unit of arable land) is highest in Country Z, at 1,500.

hardQuiz.q: Country Y’s arithmetic and physiological densities are almost the same. What does this suggest?
o: A large share of its land is arable
Very little of its land is arable
Most of its people live in cities
Its agricultural density is extremely high
hardQuiz.e: If dividing by arable land barely changes the number, most of the land is arable.

hardQuiz.q: A country has 36 million people and 90,000 square kilometers of land, of which 9,000 square kilometers is arable. What is its physiological density?
o: 4,000 people per sq km of arable land
400 people per sq km of arable land
40,000 people per sq km of arable land
1,000 people per sq km of arable land
hardQuiz.e: Physiological density is population divided by arable land: 36,000,000 / 9,000 = 4,000. Dividing by total land area gives 400, which is the arithmetic density, not the physiological density.

hardQuiz.q: A country has 9 million people, including 3.6 million farmers, and 12,000 square kilometers of arable land. What is its agricultural density?
o: 750 farmers per sq km of arable land
300 farmers per sq km of arable land
30 farmers per sq km of arable land
3,000 farmers per sq km of arable land
hardQuiz.e: Agricultural density = farmers divided by arable land = 3,600,000 / 12,000 = 300. The tempting 750 divides the whole population (9 million) by arable land, which is physiological density.

hardQuiz.q: Country A and Country B both have an arithmetic density of 400 people per sq km, but Country B’s physiological density is eight times higher. Which inference is best supported?
o: Country B has a larger total population than Country A has
Country B has a smaller share of its people working as farmers
Country B’s people depend on much less farmable land
Country B has more arable land available per person than A
hardQuiz.e: Equal arithmetic density with a higher physiological density means the same crowding is spread over less arable land. Total population cannot be inferred because the countries’ areas are not given.

hardQuiz.q: At 3:00 am Monday in Greenwich Mean Time, what is the local time in a city located at 105°E?
o: 8:00 pm Sunday, 7 hours behind GMT
10:00 am Monday, 7 hours ahead
8:00 am Monday, 5 hours ahead
6:00 pm Monday, 15 hours ahead
hardQuiz.e: 105° / 15° per hour = 7 hours, and east of Greenwich is ahead, so 3:00 am + 7 h = 10:00 am. The tempting 8:00 pm Sunday subtracts the hours, which applies to west longitudes.

hardQuiz.q: A video call starts at 3:00 am Tuesday GMT. What is the local time for a participant at 75°W?
o: 8:00 am Tuesday
10:00 pm Tuesday
10:00 pm Monday
12:00 midnight Monday
hardQuiz.e: 75° / 15° = 5 hours; west is behind GMT, so 3:00 am Tuesday minus 5 h is 10:00 pm Monday. The tempting 8:00 am Tuesday adds the hours instead of subtracting them.

hardQuiz.q: A ship sailing east from Japan toward Hawaii crosses the International Date Line at noon on Tuesday. What happens as it crosses?
o: The date becomes Wednesday, with the clock time unchanged
The date stays Tuesday, with the clock set back one hour
The date stays Tuesday, with the clock set ahead one hour
The date becomes Monday, with the clock time unchanged
hardQuiz.e: Crossing the date line eastward subtracts a day while the clock time stays the same. The tempting Wednesday choice applies the westward rule, which adds a day.

hardQuiz.q: A hiker uses a map with a scale of 1:100,000. Two trailheads are 3.5 cm apart on the map. What is the real distance between them?
o: 3.5 kilometers
about 350 kilometers
35 kilometers
350 meters
hardQuiz.e: 3.5 cm x 100,000 = 350,000 cm = 3,500 m = 3.5 km. The tempting 350 meters misplaces the decimal when converting centimeters to meters.

hardQuiz.q: A student compares a 1:24,000 map and a 1:250,000 map of the same county. Which statement is correct?
o: The 1:250,000 map shows a smaller area with more detail
The 1:24,000 map is a small-scale map covering more area
The two maps show the same area at a different paper size
The 1:24,000 map shows a smaller area with more detail
hardQuiz.e: 1/24,000 is the larger fraction, so it is the large-scale map: less area, more detail. The tempting reversal treats the bigger denominator as meaning greater detail.

hardQuiz.q: A teacher wants a world map on which Mongolia appears small and Bangladesh appears large, because each country’s size reflects its number of people. Which map type fits?
o: A cartogram scaled by population
A choropleth map shaded by population density
An isoline map of population totals by country
A proportional symbol map drawn on a Mercator base
hardQuiz.e: A cartogram distorts the area of each country to match a variable, here population. The tempting choropleth keeps the true country sizes and only changes shading.

hardQuiz.q: A choropleth map shades each U.S. state by its total number of residents over age 65. Why could it mislead a reader comparing how aged each state’s population is?
o: Choropleths cannot show numerical values, so shading categories are chosen arbitrarily
The map shows exact resident locations, which exaggerates patterns inside each state
Populous states look older even if seniors are a smaller share of their residents
Proportional symbols on the map make the largest states seem to hold more seniors
hardQuiz.e: A choropleth shades areas by one value, so totals track population size rather than the share of seniors. A rate such as percent over 65 would compare states fairly.

hardQuiz.q: Pittsburgh grew in part because of its position where the Allegheny and Monongahela rivers meet. Which statement describes its situation rather than its site?
o: Rivers and rail linked it to nearby coal fields and Midwest steel markets
It sits on a flat triangle of land at the confluence of two rivers, giving it room to build
Its coordinates are about 40°N latitude and 80°W longitude
Residents informally think of it as part of Appalachia
hardQuiz.e: Situation is a place’s location relative to other places and connections, such as access to coal and markets. The tempting confluence statement describes site, the physical character of the place itself.

hardQuiz.q: A geographer shades every Canadian census district in which most residents speak French as their first language. This kind of region is a
o: functional region, defined by flows to a central node
vernacular region, defined by popular perception
formal region, defined by a shared measurable trait
functional region, defined by a transportation network
hardQuiz.e: A formal region shares a measurable characteristic across it, here majority first language. The tempting vernacular choice applies to regions people informally name, not to ones mapped from census data.

hardQuiz.q: Delta Air Lines routes passengers through Atlanta, and the airports it serves are organized around that hub. The area served is best described as a
o: formal region, since the airports share one measurable trait
vernacular region, since travelers agree on its name
formal region, since its boundary is officially drawn
functional region, organized by flows to and from the hub
hardQuiz.e: A functional region is organized around a node and its connections, such as an airline hub. The tempting formal-region choice requires uniform traits across the area rather than links to a center.

hardQuiz.q: Seeing Western fast food, a company in India sells vegetarian-patty sandwiches and avoids beef to fit local religious norms. This best illustrates
o: stimulus diffusion
relocation diffusion
contagious diffusion
hierarchical diffusion
hardQuiz.e: Stimulus diffusion spreads the underlying idea while the original form is changed to fit the new culture. The tempting contagious diffusion implies the original product spreads unchanged to nearby people.

hardQuiz.q: In the diffusion curve, adoption grows fastest in the middle period. Which group is adopting during that rapid growth?
o: The innovators
The late adopters
Nobody; the curve is flat there
The early majority
hardQuiz.e: The steep middle part of the S-curve is when most people adopt; innovators come first and late adopters last.

hardQuiz.q: Which situation best illustrates acculturation rather than assimilation?
o: A third-generation immigrant family has lost the heritage language and adopted all local customs
A neighborhood keeps its ethnic identity and avoids contact with the host society
A Vietnamese family in Houston speaks English at work but keeps its food and holidays at home
A fashion trend spreads from large cities to smaller towns by hierarchical diffusion
hardQuiz.e: Acculturation means adopting some traits of another culture while keeping aspects of the original one. The tempting third-generation example shows assimilation, where the original culture is largely lost.

hardQuiz.q: A city plans school funding in 2029 using the 2020 national census. Which limitation of census data most directly affects that plan?
o: Census data cannot be broken down by age group, so planners must rely on sample surveys
A census counts only people who own property, so renters are left out of the totals
Census counts measure physiological density only, so numbers of farmers cannot be found
Counts grow outdated between decades and can undercount groups such as recent migrants
hardQuiz.e: A census is infrequent and may miss groups, so the data age and may be incomplete. The tempting age claim is wrong because censuses routinely report age structure.

hardQuiz.q: According to the bar graph, Country D’s population is about how many times Country A’s?
o: about 1.4 times
about 3.4 times
about 3.4 million times
about 0.3 times
hardQuiz.e: 81 ÷ 24 ≈ 3.4. The graph shows values in millions for both, so the units cancel.

hardQuiz.q: Which statement is supported by the line graph?
o: Country Q urbanized faster than Country P because it was more urban in every year shown
Both countries urbanized at the same rate over the period shown
Country P was more urban than Country Q in 1950 but less urban by 2010
Country P urbanized faster than Country Q even though Q was more urban in every year shown
hardQuiz.e: P rose from about 20% to 64% (+44 points) and Q from 50% to 80% (+30 points), so P grew faster while Q stayed higher.

hardQuiz.q: The scatterplot shows which relationship between the two variables?
o: A negative correlation: places with more arable land tend to produce less food per person
A positive correlation: places with more arable land tend to produce more food per person
No relationship, since the dots do not fall exactly on one line
A proven cause: more arable land makes food production rise in every place
hardQuiz.e: The dots rise together, a positive correlation. A scatterplot shows association, not proof of cause.

hardQuiz.q: Which country has the oldest population according to the chart?
o: Country R, with 38 percent aged 0 to 14
Country T, with 27 percent aged 0 to 14
Country S, with 64 percent aged 15 to 64
Country S, with 18 percent aged 65 and over
hardQuiz.e: The share aged 65 and over is largest in Country S. Country R’s large child share indicates a young population.

hardQuiz.q: Which country is most likely to have the heaviest burden of supporting dependent children?
o: Country S
Country T
All three equally, because each total is 100 percent
Country R
hardQuiz.e: Country R has 38 percent of its population under 15, the largest share of child dependents.

hardQuiz.q: Which projection family is most often used to map the polar regions?
o: Cylindrical
Conic
Cylindrical, because it keeps the poles the same size
Planar (azimuthal)
hardQuiz.e: Planar projections are centered on a point such as a pole; cylindrical projections like Mercator badly distort the poles.

hardQuiz.q: What is Country B’s arithmetic density, using the table (millions of people and thousands of km²)?
o: 300 people per sq km
3 people per sq km
30 people per sq km
3,000 people per sq km
hardQuiz.e: 120 million ÷ 400 thousand km² = 120,000,000 ÷ 400,000 = 300 per km².
